headline: A claimed proof that rational curves on a Fano manifold cap its Picard number, with equality only for product spaces.
scope: The claim covers every smooth complex Fano manifold of positive dimension. It gives the bound and the full equality case.
plain: A Fano manifold is a smooth, closed shape that curves positively in a precise algebraic sense. Its Picard number counts independent ways to measure curves on it. Its pseudoindex is the smallest positivity degree of any sphere-shaped curve on it. This paper claims that Picard number times pseudoindex minus one never exceeds the dimension. It also claims equality happens only for a product of identical projective spaces.
doesNot: This does not come with a computer-checked proof, and no Lean scope note exists for it.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Shigeru Mukai, index version of the bound
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to settle, in every dimension, a bound that earlier work proved only up to dimension five or under extra conditions.

explanation:
Take the projective plane P², an ordinary plane with a line at infinity added. It has dimension n = 2. A rational curve is a curve shaped like a sphere, such as a line. The anticanonical degree of a curve measures how strongly the space bends positively along it. For a line in P² that degree is 3, and no rational curve has less. The smallest such degree is called the pseudoindex, written ι. The Picard number ρ counts the independent ways to measure curves. For P², ρ = 1. So ρ(ι − 1) = 1 × 2 = 2, which equals n.

Now take P¹ × P¹, a product of two lines. Here n = 2 and ρ = 2. A line in either direction has anticanonical degree 2, so ι = 2. Then ρ(ι − 1) = 2 × 1 = 2, again equal to n. The product P¹ × P² has n = 3, ρ = 2 and ι = 2. There ρ(ι − 1) = 2, which is below 3. Blow up one point of the plane, replacing it by a small sphere. That sphere has anticanonical degree 1, so ι = 1 and ρ(ι − 1) = 0.

All of these are Fano manifolds. A Fano manifold is a smooth, closed algebraic space whose anticanonical class is ample, meaning positive on every curve. That positivity forces rational curves to exist, so ι makes sense. The generalized Mukai conjecture says ρ(ι − 1) ≤ n for every such space of positive dimension n. It adds that equality happens only for a product of ρ copies of the projective space P^(ι−1). The examples fit: P² is one copy of P², and P¹ × P¹ is two copies of P¹.

Shigeru Mukai posed the first version in 1988, using the Fano index[3]. The Fano index is the largest integer dividing the anticanonical class, and it can differ from ι[2]. Jarosław Wiśniewski introduced the pseudoindex and proved that 2ι > n + 2 forces ρ = 1[4]. Bonavero, Casagrande, Debarre and Druel stated the pseudoindex form and proved it up to dimension four[5]. Andreatta, Chierici and Occhetta extended this to dimension five[6]. Casagrande settled a broad class of toric Fano varieties, built from combinatorial data, in every dimension[7]. Novelli proved both parts whenever ι > n/3[8]. Each of these results needs a limit on dimension, symmetry or ι. The paper claims a proof with no such limit[9,1].

The approach uses quantum cohomology. Ordinary cohomology records how subspaces meet. Quantum cohomology also counts rational curves that run between them. Multiplying by a divisor class, a basic way to measure curves, then gives a matrix. Its entries mix ordinary intersection with counts of curves of each degree. A curve count of anticanonical degree d lowers codimension by d − 1[10]. Codimension is the number of conditions that cut out a subspace. Each step lowers it by at least ι − 1, and it can only fall from n to 0. So a nonzero product built from ρ independent curve degrees gives ρ(ι − 1) ≤ n.

The main obstacle is producing that nonzero product without assuming semisimplicity[11]. Semisimple roughly means the matrices split into independent one-by-one blocks. The paper first proves a lower bound for certain curve counts called point descendants[12]. A recurrence then shows that one joint eigenvalue list has ρ algebraically independent entries[13]. A trace argument turns that independence into the needed product of curve counts[14]. At equality, the paper builds chains of actual rational curves. It then applies Occhetta's description of products of projective spaces[15].

How sure is this? There is no Lean scope note for this result, so no computer proof checker has tested it. The paper claims to prove both the bound and the equality case. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. It is a single paper with no Lean scope note. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A smooth, closed algebraic space whose anticanonical class is positive on every curve.
A curve in the space shaped like a sphere, such as a line.
The smallest anticanonical degree of any rational curve in the space.
The number of independent ways to measure curves in the space.
The largest integer that divides the anticanonical class.
A way of multiplying subspaces that also counts rational curves running between them.
The number of conditions needed to cut out a subspace.
